title: Dürer’s conjecture
formal: For every bounded three-dimensional convex polytope \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with nonempty interior, is there a connected edge unfolding whose distinct face interiors do not overlap in the plane?
why: This long-standing question asks whether every convex three-dimensional shape has an edge-based planar net, a basic unresolved principle in geometric folding and representation.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The March 2026 prismatoid paper retains the general existence question; the July overlap construction does not refute it. This card uses its explicit disjoint-facet-interior convention with boundary contacts permitted, without asserting equivalence to a stricter simple-boundary requirement. The bounded source review did not independently verify the cited proofs.

progress.text: The problem source records the general convex edge-unfolding question as open and distinguishes known nonconvex obstructions.
The revised prismatoid paper retains the general prismatoid and convex edge-unfolding questions while analyzing a restricted subclass.
A preprint constructs selected unfoldings with arbitrarily high overlap; it does not show that every unfolding of any convex polytope overlaps.

sentences: The input is a convex three-dimensional polytope.
Its faces may be separated only along original edges.
The output sought is one connected planar net.
Distinct face interiors must not overlap.
Allowing cuts across faces or disconnected pieces gives a different problem.

definitions: A convex polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of real points. Its faces here are its maximal two-dimensional facets, and adjacent facets share an entire polytope edge. Choose a spanning tree of the facet adjacency graph. Make separate copies of all facets and glue only the pairs of matching edges selected by that tree, retaining the edge identifications inherited from \(P\). An edge unfolding is a map of this glued polygonal surface to \(\mathbb R^2\) whose restriction to each copied facet is a Euclidean isometry and whose restrictions agree on glued edges. Require images of the relative interiors of distinct facets to be disjoint. Contacts between boundary points are permitted; cuts may run only along original polytope edges. The glued surface and its image are connected. This is a geometric existence statement with arbitrary real coordinates, not an algorithmic runtime claim.

context_blocks.text: A net lays out the actual faces of a solid in one plane without stretching them. A cube provides familiar examples: its six squares can remain connected along selected edges and spread out without their interiors covering one another. The conjecture asks for such a choice for every convex polytope, regardless of the number, shape or arrangement of its facets.

The connected gluing pattern matters independently of overlap. Keeping a tree of facet adjacencies attaches every face to one planar assembly. It does not guarantee that faces far apart in that tree avoid one another after flattening. The existence question concerns a suitable choice of the whole pattern, not whether every possible net succeeds.

Only original polytope edges are available for cuts. Triangulating a facet and then allowing cuts on the new diagonals, slicing through face interiors, or returning disconnected pieces changes the task. Nonconvex examples without suitable unfoldings likewise do not refute a statement restricted to convex input.

This card retains its explicitly chosen nonoverlap convention: relative interiors of distinct facets must be disjoint, while boundary contacts are allowed. A requirement that the entire unfolded boundary be a simple Jordan curve is an additional condition; no equivalence to that stricter condition is assumed. The distinction is explicit in the unfolding literature.

O’Rourke’s March 2026 preprint still identifies even the general prismatoid case as unresolved. A prismatoid is a convex polytope whose vertices lie in two parallel planes. Its nested special cases concern a restricted geometric arrangement, leaving arbitrary convex polytopes outside their guarantee.

The July 2026 overlap construction finds convex polyhedra with particular edge unfoldings of arbitrarily large overlap thickness. Showing that one choice of cuts overlaps is different from showing that every choice overlaps. The latter universal failure would be needed for a counterexample to the existence question.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every convex polytope in the stated domain has a spanning tree of facet adjacencies and compatible planar facet isometries with pairwise disjoint relative interiors, or prove a counterexample in Lean: one such polytope for which every permitted gluing tree and planar realization fails. No algorithmic runtime or stricter boundary-injectivity claim is required.
